rooms.title: The Empty Floor
rooms.scene: The 47th floor is quiet except for rain against the glass. A few desks are still lit. Nothing looks obviously wrong, but the timing of a handful of ordinary events feels slightly off.
rooms.objective: Mark anything that might matter later. Some routine-looking items are not routine. Some alarming-looking items are harmless.

clues.label: Calendar invite // 09:00 AM
clues.detail: Quarterly productivity review. Created by a familiar internal display name, but the invite was modified at 02:07 AM.

clues.label: VPN status card
clues.detail: Singapore exit node active. The employee is enrolled in a corporate VPN that occasionally routes through Singapore.

clues.label: Desk phone notification
clues.detail: One MFA approval appears between several routine push notifications. The approval was accepted while the desk was unoccupied.

clues.label: Printer queue
clues.detail: A 54-page document was printed at 01:58 AM. It matches a scheduled board pack generated every Thursday.

clues.label: Wi-Fi maintenance card
clues.detail: Printed card beside the break room router. The QR destination resolves to a domain registered yesterday, but the branding matches AstraTech exactly.

clues.label: Cleaning contractor badge
clues.detail: A contractor badge accessed the floor at 01:42 AM. Building access logs show the same contractor has serviced this floor every Thursday for six months.

rooms.title: Routine Messages
rooms.scene: The employee's inbox and chat history look normal at first. Most messages are ordinary workplace noise. One or two become suspicious only when compared with timing and metadata.
rooms.objective: Look past tone and branding. Focus on what does not line up with the surrounding context.

clues.label: Benefits portal reminder
clues.detail: Professional-looking HR reminder using the normal AstraTech template. The button points to a subdomain under astratech-benefits.com, not the internal benefits provider.

clues.label: IT support chat
clues.detail: Support asks the employee to approve a sign-in prompt so they can 'finish device sync.' The account is three days old but belongs to the legitimate outsourced help desk tenant.

clues.label: Meeting transcript email
clues.detail: Sent from a trusted automated service. Attachment is a normal PDF, but it arrived two minutes after the unusual MFA approval and includes an external-sharing link never used by this team.

clues.label: Expense approval
clues.detail: Urgent subject line and unusual punctuation, but the sender, ticket number, and approval URL all match prior legitimate expense emails.

clues.label: Password expiry notice
clues.detail: No obvious spelling mistakes. The notice references the employee's actual department and manager, but the message was sent from a newly created external mailbox with a matching display name.

clues.label: Vendor invoice
clues.detail: Unexpected attachment from a supplier the employee rarely works with. Procurement records show the vendor was added legitimately last month.

rooms.title: Account Trace
rooms.scene: Authentication logs contain a mix of ordinary remote work, VPN routing, stale sessions, and a few subtle anomalies. None of the individual events are conclusive by themselves.
rooms.objective: Identify which events become risky only when viewed together.

clues.label: 02:16 // New device cookie
clues.detail: A fresh browser session appears, but the device reports the same operating system and browser family as the employee's managed laptop.

clues.label: 02:17 // Singapore login
clues.detail: Successful sign-in from Singapore. This could match the corporate VPN, but the VPN client shows no active tunnel at that exact minute.

clues.label: 02:18 // MFA accepted
clues.detail: One push approval succeeds after several ignored prompts. The employee later says they assumed it was part of a normal Outlook refresh.

clues.label: 01:52 // Password manager login
clues.detail: Successful login to the approved enterprise password manager from the managed laptop. No unusual geo or device change.

clues.label: Personal streaming login
clues.detail: A personal streaming service recorded a login using the same public IP. This looks suspicious but is unrelated to the corporate account.

clues.label: 02:19 // Refresh token issued
clues.detail: A new refresh token is issued immediately after MFA approval, then used again after the user reports closing their laptop.

rooms.title: Permission Drift
rooms.scene: Several apps have access to the account. Most permissions are normal for enterprise tools. One application looks harmless because its name resembles an approved productivity product.
rooms.objective: Separate normal enterprise access from permissions that quietly create persistence or impersonation risk.

clues.label: Notes Sync Pro
clues.detail: Requests basic profile, calendar read access, offline access, and the ability to read mail metadata. The app name is one word different from an approved tool used elsewhere in AstraTech.

clues.label: AstraDocs Connector
clues.detail: Can read files in the employee's project workspace. This scope is documented in the service catalog and was approved months ago.

clues.label: Send as user
clues.detail: Granted to a newly authorized app. The permission is buried under 'mail integration' and was approved at 02:22 AM.

clues.label: Calendar write access
clues.detail: Granted to the company's room-booking assistant. The app is signed by the verified tenant and widely used.

clues.label: Offline access
clues.detail: By itself this is common, but on the newly authorized lookalike app it allows access to continue after the browser closes.

clues.label: Export approval // 02:24
clues.detail: A bulk export was approved after hours. The approver is legitimate, but the request came from a session created two minutes after the suspicious token was issued.

rooms.title: Endpoint Noise
rooms.scene: The workstation is noisy with background services, sync jobs, browser extensions, scheduled tasks, and security tooling. The dangerous activity blends into normal enterprise behavior.
rooms.objective: Do not chase everything unusual. Find the activity that breaks the workstation's normal pattern.

clues.label: BackupAgent.exe
clues.detail: Unknown to the user and running at 02:25 AM, but the hash matches AstraTech's approved backup software and the path is signed by IT.

clues.label: Browser extension update
clues.detail: A PDF helper extension updated silently. It was installed months ago, but its publisher changed last week and it now has permission to read data on all sites.

clues.label: Cloud sync spike
clues.detail: Large outbound transfer to a major cloud provider. Normally harmless, except this employee's OneDrive client is paused and the destination account is external.

clues.label: Unsigned PowerShell window
clues.detail: A command window opened briefly. Investigation notes show the endpoint management tool legitimately used PowerShell for a patch at the same time.

clues.label: Contacts cache read
clues.detail: A process reads the local contacts cache, then several coworkers receive convincing password-reset messages minutes later.

clues.label: USB device attached
clues.detail: An encrypted corporate recovery drive was connected by the night technician and is recorded in the maintenance ticket.

rooms.title: Containment Window
rooms.scene: You have enough context to act, but every response has trade-offs. Some actions sound decisive while making the investigation worse. Others feel less dramatic but contain the attacker cleanly.
rooms.objective: Choose the response sequence you would trust in a real incident.

actions.label: Revoke sessions and refresh tokens
actions.detail: Invalidate the user's active cloud sessions and refresh tokens before resetting credentials.

actions.label: Reset password immediately
actions.detail: Force a password reset through the trusted recovery path, but do not assume this alone removes existing sessions.

actions.label: Remove the newly authorized app
actions.detail: Revoke the suspicious application's consent and review any delegated permissions it created.

actions.label: Isolate the workstation
actions.detail: Move the affected device into containment while preserving memory, logs, and artifacts for investigation.

actions.label: Block all Singapore traffic
actions.detail: Fast and dramatic, but risks breaking legitimate VPN traffic and does not address stolen sessions elsewhere.

actions.label: Shut down the laptop
actions.detail: Stops local activity, but may destroy volatile evidence and does not terminate cloud access already established.

actions.label: Notify users and preserve evidence
actions.detail: Alert affected users, preserve logs, and start the formal incident trail while containment is underway.

actions.label: Delete suspicious emails from every mailbox
actions.detail: Feels protective, but can destroy evidence before scope is understood and may not remove the original access path.
